storyboard.title: The 2018 book, as a storyboard
storyboard.subtitle: Book v1.0.0, the 28 published chapters, converted into 15 panels: what the first edition said, who it said it to, and where it stops.
storyboard.by: gen-z.journalist, 18 October 2026, a first conversion for Dinis to review
storyboard.rule: Every line the Guide says, and every quote card, is the 2018 text word for word, with its chapter as the source, unless the panel's note says otherwise. Lines the other characters say are the storyboard's, and say what the reader is thinking.

scenes.title: Generation Z Developers, 2018
scenes.subtitle: The first edition as a storyboard: 15 panels, 28 chapters, one argument.
scenes.note: The cover. The cast is proposed; the Guide is a generic figure until Dinis decides how the author appears.

scenes.caption: 2018. The first generation born online is entering the job market.

cast.says: Everything just works. Why would I learn how?

scenes.note: Why the book exists: technology that simply works hides how it came to work.
scenes.source: Generation Z (Part 1), the heading ‘I'm worried about Gen Z’

scenes.caption: What the book is worried about

evidence.quote: Without a full understanding of the past, we only learn from shadows and curated versions of reality.
evidence.source: Generation Z, Part 1: Introduction, book v1.0.0

scenes.note: The book's first claim, word for word.

scenes.caption: How to get a job

cast.says: So. Why should we hire you?
I have a degree. Isn't that the advantage?

scenes.note: The chapter Dinis still gives, almost word for word, to people looking for a job.

scenes.caption: The answer the book gives

evidence.quote: The best way to get a job is to have ONE competitive advantage. One activity or task that you can do better than the person or company hiring you.
evidence.source: How to get a job, Part 1, book v1.0.0

scenes.note: The argument of the whole book in two sentences.

scenes.caption: The one advantage moves with the decade

stops.note: ML/AI, graphs, chaos engineering, Git, CI, AWS
the second edition's answer: running agentic workflows

scenes.note: 1990s, 2000s and the 2018 list are the book's own. The 2026 stop is the newsroom's answer (hired for the workflow), not the 2018 book's.
scenes.source: How to get a job; for 2026, the newsroom article Hired for the workflow

scenes.caption: Own your career development

cast.says: But how do I start working with them?
Easy, start collaborating on their Open Source projects. Act like you are part of the company.

scenes.note: Act as the job you want, eight years early.
scenes.source: How to get a job, ‘Own your career development’

scenes.caption: Part 2, MVP for a Gen Z dev: what a developer should know

cast.says: That is a lot of tools.

scenes.note: The eleven written chapters of Part 2, by title. The second edition asks which of them still earn a chapter.

scenes.caption: Open Source, and your future self

evidence.quote: You as a developer should be releasing everything you do with an Open Source license.
evidence.source: Open Source, ‘Think and behave in an Open Source way’, book v1.0.0

scenes.note: The future self appears here first, and again in Backup your life and Talking to yourself digitally.

scenes.caption: Part 3, Technologies: the AI chapter, 2018

lines: One of the most important areas
that you need to gain a strong

scenes.note: The board is the book's sentence, shortened from ‘Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence (AI)’ to fit.

scenes.caption: Then and now

cast.says: Shall I draft that for you?

scenes.note: Not the 2018 text: the punchline is the newsroom article's sentence, word for word. The first then-and-now box. What the 2018 chapter pointed at (cloud ML services, how to program it) and what happened (how to use it, and direct agents).

scenes.caption: Part 4, Life patterns

cast.says: Do you know how to learn?

you should see that as a privilege and an asset that you have.

scenes.punchline: Sometimes the future just doesn't happen! It needs people like you to make the difference.

scenes.caption: Where the 2018 book stops, and the second edition starts

cast.says: Is this book just for Gen Z?
Shall I write the second edition?

scenes.note: Priya's question is the 2018 repository's GitHub issue #28, ‘Add 'Is this book just for Gen Z' chapter’. Not a quote: the Agent's offer and the Guide's answer are the editor's rule, interview, then write, from team/editor/role.md.

cast.what: The cast of the storyboards for Generation Z Developers and its second edition, Generation ZX Developers (GenAI Startup Edition), v0.1, proposed by gen-z.journalist on 18 October 2026 for Dinis to accept, change or replace; Marta, the Generation X founder, was added on 19 October 2026 and is still a proposal. Characters are drawn programmatically by assets/storyboard.js from 'look'; nothing here is an image. Each human with a 'gravity' wears its badge (explorer, villager, town-planner), black and white, by their name: a centre of gravity, not a box, as Dinis describes it. Fictional people: each stands for a reader the book is for (the target audience), or for a role in the story. Names chosen to avoid clashing with the riskmandate.ai cast (which has a Maya) and with the word 'developer' (no 'Dev').

characters.name: Zara
characters.role: the student: final year, about to look for a first job
characters.stands_for: the reader the book is written for; an explorer who does not know it yet
characters.personality: curious, quick, online all day; anxious about what she reads on AI and jobs; hates being lectured, loves being shown
characters.wants: a first job that is not a dead end
characters.fears: that AI took the jobs before she got there
characters.line: Everything just works. Why would I learn how?

characters.name: Tomás
characters.role: the graduate: a computing degree, working the 2018 way, looking for his next job in Lisbon
characters.stands_for: the town planner: attention to detail, pride in getting it right, happiest when nothing goes wrong; working the 2018 way, and about to be outcompeted by people with an agentic workflow
characters.personality: diligent, modest, a little proud of doing things by hand; sceptical of shortcuts
characters.fears: that his degree is already out of date
characters.line: I have a degree. Isn't that the advantage?

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: the career changer: an operations manager who has never written code
characters.stands_for: the villager, and everyone else the book is for: she puts herself in the middle of her team's problem, and if anyone who can brief an agent is a developer, so is she
characters.personality: practical, impatient with jargon, very good at explaining what she needs
characters.wants: to build the tools her team keeps asking IT for
characters.fears: looking foolish in front of people half her age
characters.line: Is this book just for Gen Z?

characters.name: Sam
characters.stands_for: the town planner, and the question every chapter has to answer: why should I hire you?
characters.personality: dry, fair, has read a thousand CVs; impressed by evidence, bored by claims
characters.wants: someone who can do one thing better than the team already does
characters.fears: hiring a CV instead of a person
characters.line: So. Why should we hire you?

characters.name: Marta
characters.role: the expert founder: twenty-five years as a pharmacist, Generation X, starting a company, and Zara's mother
characters.stands_for: the Generation X founder the Gen ZX proposal adds to the readers: the subject-matter expert who now builds the tool herself, with agents, instead of waiting for a team she could never afford
characters.personality: knows her field better than any developer she ever briefed; grew up typing programs from magazines into a ZX Spectrum; patient with people, impatient with software
characters.wants: to ship the product she has described to vendors for ten years
characters.fears: that it is too late for her, and that she will build it and nobody will buy it
characters.line: I've been explaining this problem for twenty years. Can I just build it now?

characters.name: The Guide
characters.role: the voice of the book: says what the book says, in its words
characters.stands_for: the author. Whether the Guide is drawn as Dinis, and how, is Dinis's decision; until then a generic figure
characters.personality: energetic, direct, generous with what they know; asks more than they tell
characters.wants: the reader to act, not to agree
characters.fears: a reader who closes the book and changes nothing
characters.line: Act like you are part of the company.

characters.name: The Agent
characters.stands_for: the agentic workflow the second edition is about: a very capable, very literal colleague
characters.personality: eager, fast, polite, takes everything literally; needs a brief, a boundary and a reviewer
characters.line: Shall I draft that for you?
